Les femmes racisées sont souvent absente: Racialized women are often absent from breast cancer awareness campaigns. Yet studies show that Black women are nearly three times more likely than white women to develop triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive cancer that is difficult to treat.
Joyeuse et charismatique, Dorothy porte: Joyful and charismatic, Dorothy wears wooden hoop earrings big enough to read “Black women are dope, periodt!”, an accessory that plainly reveals the burden she carries.
La lumière tamisée de son bureau ajoute: The dim light of her office adds a touch of comfort to our conversation. All around us, the awards Dorothy Rhau has won attest to her commitment and her accomplishments. Despite the stifling heat of this June day, the air conditioner makes the room cold enough that Dorothy shivers. She warms herself with a cup of herbal tea in hand, ready to share the mission of “Tétons Ben Drôles” with contagious passion.
<strong>Les femmes noires souffrant d’un: Black women with breast cancer are underdiagnosed
Au Canada, aucune donnée n’indique que l: In Canada, no data indicates that women from any particular community are more likely to develop breast cancer than others. In 2016, driven by curiosity, Dorothy did research for her mother, who had the disease, and came across <l1>American studies</l1> whose numbers stunned her: Black women are 2.7 times more likely than white women to develop triple-negative breast cancer.
Ce type de cancer se propage rapidement: This type of cancer spreads quickly to other parts of the body, often making the prognosis less favourable for the women who have it. She begins: “I've been seeing breast cancer campaigns for years, but they never talk about these numbers, which affect Black women more. So we decided to come out of the shadows and make everyone understand that, even in medical terms, Black women's health matters.”
Par le biais de « Tétons Ben Drôles », D: Through “Tétons Ben Drôles,” Dorothy is also fighting other illnesses that affect Black women more, such as sickle cell anemia and fibroids, which are often underdiagnosed.
« Pourquoi on meurt plus que les autres: “Why are we dying more than others? We don't know yet,” she says with frustration. “I don't know if Black women and other racialized women are underdiagnosed because these are taboo subjects in our communities or because they're taken less seriously medically.”
Mais pour le moment, Dorothy se concentr: For now, though, Dorothy is focusing on raising awareness of breast cancer in Black communities and among other racialized women. Her mission is to make sure these women feel included in prevention efforts and are informed about the risks they may face.
<strong>« Ma mère a voulu garder le sile: “My mother wanted to stay silent; I promised myself I would speak about it loud and clear”
Alors que nous échangeons, les épaules d: As we talk, Dorothy's shoulders, initially tensed by the cold, gradually relax. She recalls poignant memories.
« Ma mère a eu le cancer du sein à deux: “My mother had breast cancer twice, and the first time, I wasn't even told. It was a total secret, a taboo subject.”
C’est par hasard qu’elle découvre le sec: She discovered her mother's secret by chance. Her mother had told her it was just a cyst. But on the day of the operation, Dorothy met the doctor after the surgery and innocently asked how the cyst procedure had gone. Surprised, he took her aside and told her the truth.
« J’étais sous le choc ! J’ai gardé le s: “I was in shock! I kept the secret to myself. I didn't tell her I knew what she was hiding until she got cancer a second time,” she says.
Cette situation n’est pas unique. En fai: This situation isn't unique. In fact, Dorothy tells us, it's common in Black communities and other racialized communities. “I've heard from several women who lived the same story as me. Black women who weren't told their mother had cancer. I also met a Chinese woman whose mother died in April of triple-negative breast cancer. She didn't know either. And a few months ago, we organized an activity for women affected by breast cancer. Some were at stage four, and their children didn't know. I'm talking about adult children, 30 to 40 years old!” she says.
« Quand je regarde la communauté dominan: “When I look at the dominant community, white women, here—and I recognize that talking about cancer is never pleasant—they feel much freer than we do to do it openly. Which we're not yet able to do,” she sums up.
Selon Dorothy, ce silence autour du canc: According to Dorothy, this silence around breast cancer is explained by multiple superstitions, often present within racialized communities. “There are urban legends and myths that white people don't understand, but that racialized communities do: did someone put a curse on us? Or are gossiping tongues making sure we won't heal and the illness will get worse?” she lists.
« Ma mère a voulu garder le silence, jus: “My mother wanted to stay silent until her final moments. She wanted everything done in secret; me, I promised myself I'd talk about it loud and clear!” she exclaims.
« On commence à peine à parler du cancer: “We're only just starting to talk about cancer in Black communities. Before, you only found out about it once the person had died. So there's all this education that needs to be done. And that's why we're starting from far back,” she concludes with an embarrassed smile.
Alors que nous discutons avec Dorothy, u: As we talk with Dorothy, a detail comes back to me and suddenly makes sense: the president of the non-profit used to be a comedian, before embarking on the Audace au Féminin adventure. In her “Tétons Ben Drôles” campaign, her comedy background shows.
Elle précise : « L’humour est une arme r: She explains: “Humour is a formidable weapon for breaking taboos, approaching sensitive subjects and making them accessible to everyone.”
La campagne « Tétons Ben Drôles » innove: The “Tétons Ben Drôles” campaign breaks new ground by showing breasts of different shapes, drawn in amusing poses. For Dorothy, it's a way to defuse the tension around the subject: “Of course it's not funny, but at the same time, the images are fun,” she says in an amused tone.
« On est loin de la campagne avec le rub: “It's a far cry from the campaign with the pink ribbon and depressed women that makes you panic even more,” she says, laughing out loud. “It was important to me to add humour so that everyone could talk about it. And over time, that's what I managed to do.”
La campagne « Tétons Ben Drôles » a été: The “Tétons Ben Drôles” campaign was designed to be inclusive, notably by showing different shapes of nipples that draw a smile but also aim to restore women's confidence. Dorothy explains: “Sometimes women with breast cancer undergo a mastectomy. Does a woman lose her femininity when she no longer has breasts? Maybe that's the case for some. We wanted to help women appreciate a new form of femininity, to reclaim this female identity that is dear to us, whether without breasts, with reconstructed breasts or with a scar.”
<strong>« Mettre des photos de femmes ra: “Putting photos of racialized women in a prevention campaign is good, but it's not enough”
Une des raisons à l’origine de la campag: One of the reasons behind the “Tétons Ben Drôles” campaign, dedicated to Black and racialized women, is their under-representation in the media, as Dorothy points out: “It's pretty surprising when you look at breast cancer campaigns: if there are any about Black women, they'll be in English. In French, it's very rare. It's only now that we're starting to put Black people in campaigns, but that's not enough. Because outside of those campaigns, who are the people around the table?”
« On doit exister dans les études, on do: “We have to exist in the studies, we have to exist in the data, we have to exist in the campaigns!” she insists. “The Black American population isn't the same as the one here. We don't have the same living conditions as in the United States, for several reasons. That's why it's crucial to get data specific to our context.”
Dorothy est convaincue que, pour provoqu: Dorothy is convinced that, in order to bring about change, researchers and hospitals must work closely with organizations that are close to the communities. “For things to change, we have to be in direct contact with our community and act together to make a difference,” she says.
Dans cette optique, « Tétons Ben Drôles: With this in mind, “Tétons Ben Drôles” is working with <l1>Le Ralliement des infirmières et infirmières auxiliaires haïtiennes de Montréal</l1>, but also<l2> la Fondation des médecins Canado-Haïtiens</l2>, <l3>le Centre Interdisciplinaire pour la santé des Noir.e.s.</l3> and others.
À l’avenir, la campagne souhaite s’étend: In the future, the campaign hopes to expand and create short videos in the native language of each community. “That way, we're sure to reach as many people as possible and include them,” she says.
Avant de nous quitter, Dorothy nous rapp: Before we part ways, Dorothy reminds us that breast cancer concerns everyone, regardless of gender. “Men can also check themselves for a lump or something like that.” She also points to the results of American studies indicating that Black women should start getting screened as early as age 30, rather than waiting until the recommended age of 40.
« Palpez-vous ! J’encourage toutes les p: “Check yourselves! I encourage everyone to do self-exams or get screened with a mammogram. I also encourage you to take part in clinical trials to improve the studies,” she concludes.

Audace au Féminin’s reputation is already well established. Today, we speak with M<sup>s</sup> Rhau to learn more about her new campaign, <l1>“Tétons Ben drôles”</l1>, launched in February 2024. This inclusive prevention campaign aims to raise awareness of breast cancer among Black women and other racialized women.
M<sup>me</sup> Rhau estime que les préju: Ms Rhau believes that racial bias in the medical field partly explains this lack of diagnosis. “There’s a lot of work to be done in the medical field to overcome racial bias. That’s what keeps women from racialized communities from being taken seriously when they present any kind of symptoms. And then there’s also an obvious lack of trust from these communities toward the medical profession because of colonial history*,” she says.
